claims.say: Can a crash lose your $100 mid-transfer? (hook; the video answers: without a transaction a failure partway through the transfer is a problem, with one none of the steps take effect)
claims.quote: if something goes wrong partway through the operation, none of the steps executed so far will take effect

claims.say: Say Alice sends Bob $100.
claims.quote: Suppose that we want to record a payment of $100.00 from Alice's account to Bob's account.

claims.say: The bank takes $100 from Alice.
claims.quote: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100.00 WHERE name = 'Alice'

claims.say: ...then adds $100 to Bob.
claims.quote: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100.00 WHERE name = 'Bob'

claims.say: Those are several separate updates.
claims.quote: the important point is that there are several separate updates involved to accomplish this rather simple operation

claims.say: If the system fails between them, Alice is debited and Bob is never credited.
claims.quote: Nor would Alice long remain a happy customer if she was debited without Bob being credited.

claims.say: Alice would not stay a happy customer.
claims.quote: Nor would Alice long remain a happy customer if she was debited without Bob being credited.

claims.say: The fix is a transaction; it bundles those steps into a single, all-or-nothing operation (also: together, they form one all-or-nothing operation).
claims.quote: The essential point of a transaction is that it bundles multiple steps into a single, all-or-nothing operation.

claims.say: If something goes wrong partway through, none of the steps take effect. (Alice keeps her $100.)
claims.quote: if something goes wrong partway through the operation, none of the steps executed so far will take effect

claims.say: If nothing fails, all the steps take effect together.
claims.quote: whereupon all the updates become visible simultaneously

claims.say: Alice's $100 reaches Bob when nothing fails (the Alice-to-Bob payment is the transaction's updates becoming visible together).
claims.quote: The updates made so far by an open transaction are invisible to other transactions until the transaction completes, whereupon all the updates become visible simultaneously.

claims.say: Either all of it happens, or none of it.
claims.quote: A transaction is said to be atomic: from the point of view of other transactions, it either happens completely or not at all.

claims.say: A transactional database logs a transaction's updates on disk before it reports the transaction complete.
claims.quote: A transactional database guarantees that all the updates made by a transaction are logged in permanent storage (i.e., on disk) before the transaction is reported complete.

claims.say: So a completed transaction survives a crash / is not lost in a crash.
claims.quote: once a transaction is completed and acknowledged by the database system, it has indeed been permanently recorded and won't be lost even if a crash ensues shortly thereafter

claims.say: Wikipedia agrees: once committed, a transaction stays committed.
claims.quote: Durability guarantees that once a transaction has been committed, it will remain committed

claims.say: In PostgreSQL, you wrap the steps in BEGIN and COMMIT; BEGIN starts it, COMMIT completes it.
claims.quote: In PostgreSQL, a transaction is set up by surrounding the SQL commands of the transaction with BEGIN and COMMIT commands.

claims.say: The updates go in between BEGIN and COMMIT.
claims.quote: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100.00 WHERE name = 'Alice'; -- etc etc COMMIT;

claims.say: In PostgreSQL, without BEGIN, each statement runs in its own transaction.
claims.quote: If you do not issue a BEGIN command, then each individual statement has an implicit BEGIN and (if successful) COMMIT wrapped around it.

claims.say: A transaction keeps your $100 from being lost in a crash or left half moved (summary of the claims above).
claims.quote: none of the steps executed so far will take effect

claims.say: Safe transfers (CTA headline; summary of the above).
claims.quote: We need a guarantee that if something goes wrong partway through the operation, none of the steps executed so far will take effect.
